pr_body:
Inside `sendRequestContentTask` recognizes that it's invoked from a timer thread and if request content fails, unblocks `SendAsyncCore` and eventually propagates the exception from the content to the outside.


Fixes #36717
pr_comments: Why this is different than case without 100Continue? If server does not respond at all, we would also block until timeout fires, right?

> Why this is different than case without 100Continue? If server does not respond at all, we would also block until timeout fires, right?

The hang happens only if we fail to send request content after `expect100Continue` timer expires. When the timer expires, we try to send the content anyway (without 100 from the server), but it fails (due to exception in custom `HttpContent`). At that moment, in non-100 scenario, we would have already reported that exception to the caller (content gets send before reading response headers). In 100 we don't, we wait for the timeout and eventually report timeout instead of the error in the content. Also, if the content sending didn't fail, the server would reply and we wouldn't end up with timeout.

For customers, the covering the content exception with timeout is making this issue supper hard to troubleshoot.
And since we added sync scenario and throwing in case of missing sync overrides, this hang is now much more probable to happen.

issue_context.title: Faulty request HttpContent might causes a hang in expect 100 Continue scenario
issue_context.body:
Concerns only **HTTP/1.1**, both sync and async scenarios and only if the **server does not reply with 100 Continue** status line.

The client sends headers with `Expect: 100-continue` and starts a [`expect100Timer`](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/master/src/libraries/System.Net.Http/src/System/Net/Http/SocketsHttpHandler/HttpConnection.cs#L460). Because the server doesn't send `100 Continue`, the timer [expires](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/master/src/libraries/System.Net.Http/src/System/Net/Http/SocketsHttpHandler/HttpConnection.cs#L778) and starts [sending the request content](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/master/src/libraries/System.Net.Http/src/System/Net/Http/SocketsHttpHandler/HttpConnection.cs#L787). If the content is faulty (e.g. throwing NSE in sync scenario due to missing sync override), no request body is sent and the server might never reply. As a result, `HttpConnection` keeps waiting for the [status line](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/master/src/libraries/System.Net.Http/src/System/Net/Http/SocketsHttpHandler/HttpConnection.cs#L499) indefinitely. If there's a request timeout and the connection gets [torn down](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/master/src/libraries/System.Net.Http/src/System/Net/Http/SocketsHttpHandler/HttpConnection.cs#L749), the original exception from the faulty `HttpContent` gets lost. This might cause serious issues while trying to troubleshoot this problem.

Note that this is rather corner case scenario: faulty custom `HttpContent` + Expect: 100-continue + server not replying at all without a request body.

Possible fixes:
- Similar to HTTP/2 behavior, i.e.: using [`WaitAny`](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/master/src/libraries/System.Net.Http/src/System/Net/Http/SocketsHttpHandler/Http2Connection.cs#L1723). Although this might prove challenging in the sync scenario where the status line parsing is synchronous. It would have to be reverted back to async for the `Expect: 100` case.
- Similar to cancellation, i.e.: tearing down the connection if the expect100Timer expired and `HttpContent` sending failed. However the exception from the [`sendRequestContentTask`](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/master/src/libraries/System.Net.Http/src/System/Net/Http/SocketsHttpHandler/HttpConnection.cs#L463) should be picked up in the final [exception handling](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/master/src/libraries/System.Net.Http/src/System/Net/Http/SocketsHttpHandler/HttpConnection.cs#L659).

cc: @scalablecory @stephentoub

review_comments:
Is this needed?

Shouldn't the default `SerializeToStream(stream, context, cancellationToken)` end up calling `SerializeToStream(stream, context)`?

TL;DR yes

This is the only sync implementation we provide for `ThrowingContent`. The one in shared code is async and there's now automatic/default sync-over-async in any of our `HttpContent` classes.

This might actually block, the `sendRequestContentTask` might still not be finished - the `Dispose` called from `SendRequestContentWithExpect100ContinueAsync` might have already propagated and manifested in an exception here while the method itself hasn't finished yet.

The very similar race condition happens in HTTP/2 as well. The exception caused by:
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/bff243c86ca5e0a9467cbb4a8b9bad6aeb90513e/src/libraries/System.Net.Http/src/System/Net/Http/SocketsHttpHandler/Http2Stream.cs#L236
might be propagated 'faster' that the task completion of `SendRequestBodyAsync` resulting in `HttpRequestException` instead of the original exception from `HttpContent` serialization.

I feel inclined to forgo the blocking here and propagate the exception only if the task has already finished. Kind of best-effort, but not worth the complications. In the worst case scenario, the content exception will only get logged.
@scalablecory, @stephentoub any input on this?

If we forgo the blocking, is there any risk of user code throwing an exception here and us not bubbling it up? Logging should only be relied on as an "also" where some other actionable exception/status is being communicated elsewhere.

Since this is an exceptional case, I think I'd be okay with blocking here.

> is there any risk of user code throwing an exception here and us not bubbling it up? 

Yes, it happens in the tests on CI. It's what I'm describing above. The connection `Dispose` propagation might be faster than the completion of `sendRequestContentTask`. Effectively bubbling up `HttpRequestException` instead of the one thrown by the content.

As I said, very similar thing happens in HTTP/2. There wasn't and isn't any hang problem, but sometimes the exception from abort is faster than completion of request sending task and we bubble up the "wrong" exception. This already exists, I just caught it with my new test.

If we do want to bubble up the right exception (the one from request content sending), I'd need change the HTTP/2 flow as well.

I also have an alternative solution, which tears down the connection after `sendRequestContentTask` finishes (inside the `expect100Continue` timer callback) but it requires using a closure for the callback (chicken-egg problem with `sendRequestContentTask` and the timer instance). I can open WIP PR with it if you want to see it?

>> This might actually block, the sendRequestContentTask might still not be finished - the Dispose called from SendRequestContentWithExpect100ContinueAsync might have already propagated and manifested in an exception here while the method itself hasn't finished yet.

I might be missing something, but I don't see how `Dispose` could has already manifested itself in this case. Caller is waiting on this thread (in `await` or `GetResult()` and can only **here** observe an exception thrown from  `SendRequestContentWithExpect100ContinueAsync` -> `SendRequestContentAsync`. Or, are you talking about the case when `Dispose` has been called from some other place on a different thread?

Yes, `SendRequestContentWithExpect100ContinueAsync` is triggered via `expect100Timer` from a different thread. It disposes the connection, unblocking the `SendAsyncCore` here, while the task itself hasn't finished yet.
